It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Quito, Ecuador at 2026-07-14 07:19 -05 (UTC-0500) (2026-07-14T12:19:00Z in UTC), at latitude -0.1807 degrees and longitude -78.4678 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 13.738 degrees and its azimuth is 67.661 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 10.484 degrees and its azimuth is 65.013 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 0.09 percent illuminated, 3.445 degrees from the Sun, and 359152.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the specific data you provided, the short answer is: **It is extremely unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can breathe a sigh of relief:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Contrast)
The biggest factor here is the **Sky Brightness**. You mentioned it is "bright daylight." In astronomy, the ability to see an object depends on its brightness relative to the background. 
*   The Sun is currently at an altitude of about 13.7 degrees. At this position, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight, creating a very bright blue sky.
*   The Moon is only 10.4 degrees up, meaning it is sitting very low in the sky, right in the thickest, brightest part of the atmosphere.

### 2. The Phase of the Moon
You noted that the Moon is only **0.09% illuminated**. This means it is in its "New Moon" phase. 
*   A New Moon is positioned almost directly between the Earth and the Sun.
*   Because it is not reflecting much sunlight toward you, it has very little "intrinsic" brightness to compete with the surrounding daylight.

### 3. Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only **3.445 degrees** away from the Sun. 
*   In visual terms, the Sun covers about 0.5 degrees of the sky. 
*   This means the Moon is sitting in the "glare" of the Sun. Even if the Moon were full, it would be almost impossible to see it this close to the Sun during the day because the Sun's light overwhelms everything in that immediate vicinity of the sky.

### 4. The "Ordinary Eyesight" Factor
Since you are using unaided eyesight, your pupils will be constricted due to the bright daylight. This further reduces your ability to pick out a faint, 0.09% illuminated sliver of rock against a bright morning sky.

**Conclusion:**
Because the Moon is nearly invisible (New Moon phase), sitting in the direct glare of the Sun, and being viewed against a bright daylight sky, **it will effectively be invisible to you.** You shouldn't worry about spotting it!
